stem: A study on the effectiveness of a new psychological therapy for depression reports the results using a 'completer analysis' rather than intention-to-treat. Of 200 patients randomised, 150 completed the treatment. The authors state that the therapy is highly effective based on the completers. Which statement BEST describes the potential bias?
options: Completer analysis overestimates treatment effects because patients who drop out tend to have worse outcomes — this is SELECTIVE ATTRITION BIAS
Completer analysis is more conservative and underestimates treatment effects
ITT analysis should never be used because it dilutes treatment effects
Completer analysis is preferable for efficacy trials
The dropouts are not relevant to the study conclusion
distractors_rationale: CORRECT. Attrition bias occurs when participants who drop out of a trial differ systematically from those who complete it. Patients who drop out typically have: (1) POORER response to treatment (non-responders may be more likely to leave); (2) MORE SIDE EFFECTS (leading to discontinuation); (3) WORSENING of the condition (especially in placebo groups). By excluding these patients, a COMPLETER (or per-protocol) analysis OVERESTIMATES the treatment effect because it only includes the 'survivors' who tolerated the treatment and/or improved. This is why INTENTION-TO-TREAT analysis is the GOLD STANDARD — it includes ALL randomised participants, regardless of what happened after randomisation. ITT preserves the benefits of randomisation and provides a CONSERVATIVE estimate of the treatment effect — closer to what would be seen in real-world practice.
ITT analysis is the more CONSERVATIVE approach (produces a smaller, more realistic effect estimate). Completer analysis OVERESTIMATES the effect (not underestimates).
ITT analysis is the preferred primary analysis for superiority trials. It is NOT 'never used' — it is the STANDARD. The CONSORT statement requires ITT analysis as the primary analysis.

EFFICACY trials (testing whether a treatment works under ideal conditions) may use per-protocol as a SENSITIVITY analysis, but ITT is the PRIMARY analysis. EFFICACY vs EFFECTIVENESS: efficacy = does it work in controlled conditions? Effectiveness = does it work in the real world?
Dropouts are highly relevant — they may differ systematically from completers, and their outcomes need to be accounted for.
teaching_point: ITT vs per-protocol vs as-treated — three analysis populations: (1) INTENTION-TO-TREAT (ITT): all randomised participants analysed in their allocated group. INCLUDES dropouts, cross-overs, and non-adherent patients. Preserves randomisation. CONSERVATIVE (dilutes the treatment effect). Gold standard. (2) MODIFIED ITT (mITT): all randomised patients who received at least one dose of study drug. Used in pharma trials when patients are randomised but never treated. (3) PER-PROTOCOL (PP): only patients who completed the trial as per protocol and had no major protocol violations. ATTENTION: it INCLUDING THOSE WHO DROPPED OUT because they WORSENED. (4) AS-TREATED: patients analysed by the treatment they actually received (not their allocated group). BIASED — patients who switch treatments are systematically different from those who don't. HANDLING MISSING DATA: (1) Last observation carried forward (LOCF) — ASSUMES NO CHANGE from the last observation (problematic in deteriorating patients). (2) Mixed models for repeated measures (MMRM) — appropriate method that accounts for the pattern of missing data. (3) Multiple imputation — uses observed data to estimate missing values. (4) Pattern mixture models — assume different outcome trajectories for completers vs dropouts. CONSORT guidelines require reporting of dropouts and their reasons for each group.
source: CONSORT 2010 statement; Altman DG (1991); NICE guidelines manual

stem: A Kaplan-Meier survival curve is presented from a study comparing lithium vs placebo for bipolar maintenance. The x-axis shows 'Time (months)' and the y-axis shows 'Proportion without relapse'. At 12 months, the lithium group shows 75% without relapse compared to 45% in the placebo group. Which statement BEST interprets this survival curve?
options: 75% of the lithium group completed the study
At 12 months, 75% of patients randomised to lithium had NOT RELAPSED — this is a time-to-event analysis that accounts for dropouts and different follow-up durations
The medication improved survival
25% of the lithium group had a side effect
The study is underpowered
distractors_rationale: The curve shows the probability of NOT relapsing over time — it does not show the proportion who completed the study (some patients may have been censored for reasons other than relapse).

CORRECT. Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival curves are a method for analysing TIME-TO-EVENT data. They are used when: (1) The outcome is an EVENT (relapse, death, hospitalisation, response); (2) Follow-up time varies between individuals; (3) Some patients are CENSORED (they are lost to follow-up or the study ends before they have the event). The KM estimator calculates the cumulative probability of 'surviving' (not having the event) over time, at each time point when an event occurs. The curve shows the PROPORTION of patients who HAVE NOT YET HAD THE EVENT at each time point. CENSORING: represented by tick marks on the curve. Patients are censored when they: complete the study without the event, drop out, or die from another cause. Important: censored patients are included in the analysis until their censoring time — their data is NOT lost. The KM curve adjusts for varying follow-up.
The term 'survival' in KM analysis means 'time to event' — it does not necessarily mean mortality. It can be 'relapse-free survival', 'hospitalisation-free survival', etc.
The curve does not show side effects.
You cannot assess power from a survival curve alone.
teaching_point: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis — HIGH-YIELD for MRCPsych: Data needed: (1) TIME to event (e.g., days since randomisation); (2) EVENT indicator (did the relapse occur? 1 = yes, 0 = censored). CENSORING: occurs when the event of interest has NOT been observed before the end of the study, loss to follow-up, or withdrawal. Assumption of KM: NON-INFORMATIVE CENSORING — patients censored at time t have the same prognosis as those still being followed (a strong assumption that should be tested). COMPARING GROUPS: LOG-RANK TEST — tests whether the survival curves differ significantly between groups. HAZARD RATIO (HR): the ratio of the hazard (risk of event per unit time) in one group relative to another. HR = 0.5 = the treatment reduces the hazard of relapse by 50% at any given time point. HR is the most common effect measure for time-to-event data. COX PROPORTIONAL HAZARDS REGRESSION: allows testing the effect of multiple covariates on survival, and estimating adjusted hazard ratios. Assumption: PROPORTIONAL HAZARDS — the hazard ratio between groups is constant over time (tested by Schoenfeld residuals, or by checking crossing KM curves). CROSSING KM curves indicate that the proportional hazards assumption is violated. Example: antipsychotic vs placebo — early curves may be similar (placebo group benefits from intensive monitoring), then diverge.
source: Kaplan EL & Meier P (1958) Nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations; BMJ statistical notes; Altman DG

stem: A researcher wants to examine the relationship between childhood trauma (measured as a continuous score on the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire — CTQ) and adult depression (measured as a continuous score on the PHQ-9) while controlling for age, gender, and socioeconomic status. The outcome (PHQ-9) is normally distributed. Which statistical analysis is MOST appropriate?
options: Simple linear regression
Multiple linear regression
Logistic regression
Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
Factor analysis
distractors_rationale: Simple linear regression would examine the relationship between ONE predictor (CTQ) and ONE outcome (PHQ-9) — it does NOT control for confounders.

CORRECT. Multiple linear regression is appropriate when: (1) The OUTCOME variable is CONTINUOUS and NORMALLY DISTRIBUTED (PHQ-9 score); (2) There are MULTIPLE PREDICTOR variables (CTQ score, age, gender, SES); (3) You want to examine the INDEPENDENT effect of each predictor ON the outcome while CONTROLLING FOR (adjusting for) the other variables. The regression equation: PHQ-9 = β₀ + β₁(CTQ) + β₂(age) + β₃(gender) + β₄(SES) + ε. β₁ is the REGRESSION COEFFICIENT for CTQ — it represents the change in PHQ-9 for a 1-unit increase in CTQ, HOLDING AGE, GENDER, AND SES CONSTANT. Multiple regression can include: continuous predictors, categorical predictors (dummy-coded), and interaction terms. Assumptions: (1) Linear relationship between predictors and outcome; (2) Independence of residuals; (3) Homoscedasticity (equal variance of residuals); (4) Normally distributed residuals; (5) No multicollinearity (predictors not too highly correlated).
Logistic regression is for BINARY (dichotomous) outcomes (e.g., depressed vs not depressed), not continuous outcomes.
ANOVA compares means between GROUPS — it is not designed for a continuous predictor like CTQ score.

Factor analysis is a DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION technique — it identifies latent constructs underlying multiple observed variables. It is not for testing the relationship between an exposure and outcome.
teaching_point: Regression analysis — choosing the right type: (1) LINEAR REGRESSION: outcome = CONTINUOUS + normally distributed. (2) LOGISTIC REGRESSION: outcome = BINARY (0/1). (3) COX REGRESSION: outcome = TIME-TO-EVENT (survival). (4) POISSON REGRESSION: outcome = COUNT DATA (e.g., number of hospitalisations). (5) ORDERED LOGISTIC REGRESSION: outcome = ORDINAL (mild/moderate/severe). (6) MULTINOMIAL LOGISTIC REGRESSION: outcome = CATEGORICAL with 3+ unordered categories. (7) MULTILEVEL / HIERARCHICAL REGRESSION: data with clustering (patients within therapists, students within schools). Regression coefficients: (1) UNSTANDARDISED (β): change in outcome per unit change in predictor — in the original units. (2) STANDARDISED (β): change in outcome in STANDARD DEVIATION UNITS per 1 SD change in predictor — allows comparison of effect sizes across different predictors. R²: proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictors. ADJUSTED R²: penalises for adding extra predictors. MODEL FIT: F-test (overall model significance), AIC/BIC (information criteria for comparing models). MULTICOLLINEARITY: predictors highly correlated (>0.8) can inflate standard errors. VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) > 10 indicates serious multicollinearity. INTERACTIONS: testing whether the effect of one predictor depends on another (e.g., does the effect of childhood trauma differ by gender?).
source: Altman DG (1991) Practical Statistics for Medical Research; Field A (2018) Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics

stem: A Cochrane review on 'SSRIs vs placebo for depression in children and adolescents' includes 17 RCTs and finds a statistically significant benefit for SSRIs (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.2 to 1.9), but with a SLIGHT increase in the risk of suicidal ideation (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.5). The GRADE quality of evidence was rated as 'MODERATE' because of concerns about PUBLICATION BIAS. Which of the following would be the MOST appropriate STRENGTH of recommendation for using SSRIs in this population?
options: Strong recommendation FOR treatment
Strong recommendation AGAINST treatment
Weak (conditional) recommendation FOR treatment, reflecting the need to balance potential benefits against small but important harms
No recommendation can be made
Recommendation for monitoring only
distractors_rationale: A strong recommendation means that most patients would want the intervention and it should be offered. Given the small effect size (OR 1.5) and the harm signal (increased suicidality), a STRONG recommendation is not appropriate.

A strong recommendation AGAINST treatment would imply that the harms clearly outweigh benefits. The evidence shows a MODEST BENEFIT (OR 1.5) alongside a SMALL RISK of harm (OR 1.7). The balance is close — this requires a WEAK recommendation, not a strong one against.

CORRECT. GRADE distinguishes between STRONG and WEAK recommendations. STRONG RECOMMENDATION = 'most patients should receive this intervention' (using 'offer' or 'do not offer'). WEAK (CONDITIONAL) RECOMMENDATION = 'different choices may be appropriate for different patients, based on their values and preferences' (using 'consider'). This is a CLASSIC weak recommendation scenario: (1) The BENEFIT is MODEST (OR 1.5 — the NNT for SSRIs in adolescent depression is ~10-12); (2) There is a POTENTIAL FOR HARM (increased suicidal ideation — NNH ~100-200 for serious suicide-related events); (3) PATIENT PREFERENCES are important — some families will accept the small risk of suicidality for the benefit of treating depression; others will not. A weak recommendation gives clinicians and patients room to discuss the trade-offs. NICE NG134 recommends FLUOXETINE as the only SSRI for adolescent depression, starting at 10mg. The FDA black box warning states: 'Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults.' The warning applies to SSRIs as a class, but the absolute risk is low (NNH ~200 for serious events).
A recommendation CAN be made — it is a weak recommendation FOR treatment.
The recommendation should be active ('consider fluoxetine'), not passive monitoring.
teaching_point: Strength of recommendations — GRADE framework: Factors that STRENGTHEN a recommendation: (1) High-quality evidence; (2) Large effect size; (3) Benefits clearly outweigh harms and burdens; (4) Low resource use/cost-effective; (5) Consistent patient values; (6) Equity considerations. Factors that WEAKEN a recommendation: (1) Low-quality evidence; (2) Small/moderate effect; (3) Benefits and harms are closely balanced; (4) High resource use; (5) Variation in patient values; (6) Implementation barriers. NICE uses a simplified system: (1) 'OFFER' = strong recommendation (most patients should receive it); (2) 'CONSIDER' = weak recommendation (requires discussion); (3) 'DO NOT OFFER' = strong recommendation against. There is also a category for 'ONLY IN RESEARCH' (the evidence is insufficient). The SUICIDALITY controversy: the FDA meta-analysis (2004) found that SSRIs doubled the risk of suicidal ideation in children/adolescents (OR ~1.7, absolute risk ~2-3% vs ~1-2% for placebo). The FDA issued a BLACK BOX WARNING (2004, updated 2007). Subsequent research (Lu et al., 2014 — BMJ) suggested that the warning may have reduced SSRI prescribing and INCREASED suicide rates in young people (the 'unintended consequences' of the black box warning). The current consensus: SSRIs (specifically fluoxetine) are effective and relatively safe for adolescent depression when monitored carefully. The risk-benefit ratio favours treatment for moderate-severe depression.
source: GRADE working group (Guyatt et al., 2008); NICE NG134; FDA black box warning (2004); Lu CY et al. (2014) BMJ

stem: A researcher is testing whether a new cognitive remediation therapy improves cognitive function in schizophrenia. They test 10 different cognitive outcomes (memory, attention, executive function, processing speed, etc.). After the study, they find that only ONE outcome (verbal memory) is statistically significant (p = 0.04). The other 9 are non-significant. Which of the following is the MOST important concern about this finding?
options: The effect size is probably very large
The significant finding may be due to CHANCE due to MULTIPLE COMPARISONS — the probability of at least one significant result by chance when testing 10 independent outcomes is 40%
The sample size is too large
The therapy is definitely effective for verbal memory
The non-significant results need not be reported
distractors_rationale: An isolated significant p-value among many non-significant ones suggests the significant result may be a FALSE POSITIVE, not a large effect.

CORRECT. This is the MULTIPLE COMPARISONS problem. When testing 10 independent null hypotheses at α = 0.05, the probability of finding AT LEAST ONE 'significant' result by CHANCE ALONE is: 1 − (0.95)¹⁰ = 1 − 0.599 = 0.401 (40%). So there is a 40% chance of at least ONE false positive finding. Given that only 1 out of 10 outcomes is significant, and that the p-value is marginal (0.04), the most parsimonious explanation is that this is a CHANCE FINDING. The finding should be considered EXPLORATORY (hypothesis-generating) until independently replicated. CORRECTIONS for multiple testing: (1) BONFERRONI — α/n (most conservative; α/10 = 0.005, so p = 0.04 would NOT be significant); (2) HOLM'S SEQUENTIAL BONFERRONI — less conservative than Bonferroni; (3) FALSE DISCOVERY RATE (FDR, Benjamini-Hochberg) — controls the expected proportion of false positives among the significant results; (4) PERMUTATION TESTS — non-parametric. The primary outcome should be PRE-SPECIFIED in the trial registration. All outcomes should be reported (not selected). The difference between 'exploratory' and 'confirmatory' analysis: CONFIRMATORY = pre-specified hypothesis, primary outcome, analysis plan
A large sample would INCREASE the chance of finding a true effect — it does not cause false positives.
Without correction for multiplicity, it is premature to claim the therapy is effective for verbal memory.

The non-significant results MUST be reported — selective reporting of significant outcomes is a form of RESEARCH MISCONDUCT (outcome reporting bias). The CONSORT statement requires all outcomes to be reported.
teaching_point: Multiple comparisons — essential concept for interpreting RCTs: 'TORTURE THE DATA LONG ENOUGH AND IT WILL CONFESS' (Ronald Coase). The MULTIPLE COMPARISONS PROBLEM arises whenever multiple statistical tests are performed on the same data. CORRECTIONS: (1) BONFERRONI CORRECTION — α* = α/n (e.g., 0.05/10 = 0.005). Very CONSERVATIVE — increases Type II errors. (2) HOLM-BONFERRONI — sequential: test the smallest p-value against α/n, the next smallest against α/(n-1), etc. (3) BENJAMINI-HOCHEM FDR — controls the proportion of false positives among the significant results (less conservative). (4) PRE-REGISTRATION — specifying the PRIMARY OUTCOME and ANALYSIS PLAN BEFORE data collection prevents selective reporting. (5) PRIMARY vs SECONDARY OUTCOMES: the primary outcome is the SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT outcome — the study is powered for this. Secondary outcomes are EXPLORATORY. (6) ADJUSTMENT for MULTIPLICITY should be pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan. NICE guidance: 'Where outcomes have not been specified as primary or secondary, or where the analysis has not adjusted for multiple testing, the results should be interpreted with caution.' In this study, the primary outcome was not pre-specified, and 10 outcomes were tested — the single significant result is likely a Type I error.
source: Altman DG (1991); Perneger TV (1998) What's wrong with Bonferroni adjustments? BMJ; BMJ statistical notes

stem: Which of the following describes the key difference between a SYSTEMATIC REVIEW and a NARRATIVE (traditional) LITERATURE REVIEW?
options: A systematic review is always written by more authors
A narrative review is more objective
A systematic review uses a PRE-SPECIFIED, TRANSPARENT, and REPRODUCIBLE methodology to identify, appraise, and synthesise all available evidence on a focused question
A narrative review includes a meta-analysis
A systematic review can only include RCTs
distractors_rationale: Number of authors is not the distinguishing feature.
A narrative review is MORE SUBJECTIVE (author's opinion, selective citation, no pre-specified methods). A systematic review is more OBJECTIVE.

CORRECT. The defining features of a SYSTEMATIC REVIEW are: (1) PRE-SPECIFIED research question (e.g., PICO format); (2) COMPREHENSIVE search strategy (multiple databases, trial registries, grey literature); (3) TRANSPARENT inclusion/exclusion criteria (documented and reproducible); (4) SYSTEMATIC ASSESSMENT of study quality (risk of bias); (5) SYNTHESIS of findings — either NARRATIVE or QUANTITATIVE (meta-analysis). A systematic review is essentially a 'study of studies' that applies the same scientific rigour to reviewing literature as would be applied to conducting a new study. The PROSPERO registry (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews) is used to PRE-REGISTER systematic review protocols, preventing duplication and selective reporting.

A meta-analysis is a STATISTICAL SYNTHESIS of data from multiple studies — it is OPTIONAL within a systematic review. Many systematic reviews cannot pool data due to heterogeneity (different populations, outcomes, or study designs).

A systematic review can include ANY study design appropriate to the research question — RCTs (for efficacy), cohort (for prognosis), case-control (for rare side effects), qualitative studies (for patient experience). The study design included depends on the research question.
teaching_point: Systematic reviews vs narrative reviews: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW: Pre-specified question, comprehensive search (multiple databases + grey literature), explicit inclusion criteria, quality assessment, transparent methods, reproducible, PRISMA checklist. NARRATIVE REVIEW: Broad topic, selective search (may be biased), no explicit inclusion criteria, no formal quality assessment, subjective summary, not reproducible. META-ANALYSIS: the statistical combination of results from two or more separate studies. It can be a part of a systematic review but is not the same thing. COCHRANE REVIEWS: the gold standard of systematic reviews — produced by the Cochrane Collaboration. They have rigorous methodology, pre-specified protocols, and are updated regularly. PRISMA: (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) — a 27-item checklist for reporting systematic reviews. Includes the PRISMA flow diagram documenting the number of studies at each stage. AMSTAR-2: (A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews) — a tool for assessing the METHODOLOGICAL QUALITY of systematic reviews. Includes 16 items (critical domains: protocol registration, comprehensive search, risk of bias assessment, appropriate meta-analysis methods, publication bias).
source: PRISMA 2020 statement; Cochrane Handbook; Higgins JPT et al. (2019) Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews

stem: A healthcare trust implements a new clinical pathway for the management of patients presenting with self-harm to the emergency department. The team measures the proportion of patients receiving a psychosocial assessment within 24 hours, BEFORE and AFTER the implementation of the pathway. This type of study is known as a:
options: Randomised controlled trial
Cohort study
Before-and-after study (interrupted time series or uncontrolled before-and-after)
Case-control study
Cross-sectional study
distractors_rationale: There was no randomisation — all patients received the pathway after implementation.
Cohort studies follow a group defined by exposure — this study defines groups by TIME PERIOD (before vs after), not exposure.

CORRECT. A BEFORE-AND-AFTER (pre-post) study measures an outcome (proportion receiving psychosocial assessment) in the same population before and after an intervention (the new pathway). This is a WEAK STUDY DESIGN because it cannot control for SECULAR TRENDS (other changes happening over the same time period — e.g., new guidelines, increased awareness, other service changes). A more robust version is INTERRUPTED TIME SERIES (ITS) — where multiple time points are measured before and after the intervention. ITS can detect whether the intervention caused a CHANGE IN LEVEL (immediate effect) and/or CHANGE IN TREND (slope) compared to the pre-intervention period. ITS is the strongest QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL design for evaluating service-level interventions where randomisation is not feasible. OTHER QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL DESIGNS: (1) Difference-in-Differences (DiD) — compares the change in the intervention group to the change in a control group. (2) Controlled before-and-after (CBA) — with a comparison group. (3) Regression discontinuity — assignment to treatment by a cut-off score. (4) Propensity score matching — matching treated and untreated individuals on observed characteristics.
No — cases and controls are not selected from the same population at the same time.
No — data are collected at two time points, not one.
teaching_point: Study designs for evaluating service-level interventions: (1) RANDOMISED (individual or cluster) — gold standard, but may not be feasible for service-level changes. (2) INTERRUPTED TIME SERIES (ITS) — multiple measures before and after; can detect changes in LEVEL and TREND; controls for secular trends; uses segmented regression analysis. (3) CONTROLLED BEFORE-AFTER (CBA) — includes a control group not receiving the intervention. (4) BEFORE-AFTER WITHOUT CONTROL — weakest design, cannot rule out secular trends. (5) STEPPED-WEDGE DESIGN — intervention is rolled out sequentially across clusters over time; eventually ALL clusters receive the intervention. This is increasingly used for service evaluations. The NICE guidelines manual prefers RCT evidence but acknowledges that for service-level interventions, well-conducted ITS and CBA studies are acceptable. The QUALITY IMPROVEMENT (QI) framework uses the PDSA cycle (Plan-Do-Study-Act) and run charts (with statistical process control) rather than classical hypothesis testing. NICE guidance on self-harm (NG225): all patients presenting with self-harm should receive a psychosocial assessment at presentation or within 24 hours.
source: NICE NG225: Self-harm; Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) guidance on ITS; BMJ Quality & Safety
